content.text: Node.js runs your JavaScript on one thread per process, and a CPU-heavy function really does freeze that process. But I/O goes to the operating system and a worker pool, and CPU work can move to worker threads, extra processes or a job queue, so the limit is how you write code, not the size of the app. This roadmap takes you from the event loop to running Node at scale in five stages, with a project and the books for each.

A team's Node.js API handles its normal traffic with room to spare. Then a customer asks for a yearly report, and for several seconds every request times out, even the health check. In the incident channel someone writes the usual verdict: Node is single-threaded, it can't do heavy work, we should rewrite the service in Go. The CPU profile tells a different story: one handler built a huge CSV in a synchronous loop and held the event loop the whole time. Moving that job off the main thread fixed it without a rewrite.
The belief: Node.js is single-threaded, so it can only handle small apps, and any heavy work will freeze the whole server no matter what you do.

Half of it is true, and the Node.js docs say so. A single Node.js process runs its JavaScript on one thread and uses one CPU core for it, and CPU-bound work such as resizing images, hashing or parsing huge payloads ties up that thread and makes the whole application unresponsive.
lets Node.js do non-blocking I/O by handing work to the operating system kernel whenever it can, and the
Don't Block the Event Loop guide

explains that Node.js also keeps a worker pool for file system calls, DNS lookups and some crypto and compression work. Its scalability comes from using few threads for many clients. For CPU work there are three built-in tools:

for other programs. "No matter what you do" is wrong: there's a lot you can do, and learning it is the job.
What a Node.js backend engineer really does

Most work is HTTP APIs and services: endpoints with validation and authorization, database queries, caching, calls to third-party APIs, background jobs, and tests for all of it. In production you watch latency, memory and event loop delay, run several instances behind a load balancer, and find the occasional function that blocks the loop. NestJS, a framework that runs on top of Express or Fastify, adds modules and dependency injection, so knowing both the framework and what sits underneath it pays off.
The stages from zero to senior

This roadmap applies to Node.js 26, the current LTS line (the docs say production apps should run only Active or Maintenance LTS releases), with TypeScript 7, NestJS 12, Express 5 and PostgreSQL 19, as of November 2026. Durations assume about 10 hours a week; at 20 hours, expect roughly half.

Node.js runs your JavaScript on one thread per process, but I/O happens in the kernel and a worker pool, which is why it serves many clients with few threads.
CPU-heavy work does block the event loop; move it to worker threads, separate processes or a job queue.
Learn JavaScript and the event loop first, SQL before an ORM, and Express before NestJS.
Measure event loop delay and profile before you add servers or plan a rewrite.
